messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Elena Weiss is a 73-year-old QA engineer who has spent decades building her life around precision, predictability, and control. In the first sessions, she described a childhood marked by physical abuse from a male caregiver she had depended on. What stands out in the way she tells it is how little narrative flow there is. She does not tell a story so much as produce stark, still images: his hand closing on her arm, the angle of a hallway lamp, dirt on the floor near a baseboard, the sharp shift in his body before he struck. At moments she can summon these scenes with photographic clarity, “like snapshots laid out in front of me,” but when asked to put them into words she falters, stares ahead, and says she knows exactly what happened yet cannot find language for it. At other times she recalls the same moments with a disturbing numbness, as though she were describing something that happened to another child. Even now, she returns to one unbearable conclusion: she was betrayed by someone she trusted, and she has never forgiven herself for not doing more to stop it.

Over the years, Elena came to believe that bad things happen without warning and that she cannot stop them. Uncertainty has become especially difficult for her. If a meeting at work is moved without explanation, if her husband says, “We need to talk later,” if she does not know who will be present in a room, she feels a familiar drop inside her. Funerals and cemeteries are particularly potent. She avoids memorial services when she can, but when attendance feels unavoidable, the sight of men in dark suits standing quietly near graves can leave her feeling as if she is no longer fully in the present. Being alone with men is worst of all. Even now, when a male contractor lingers in an office doorway or a male colleague stays behind after others leave, her body reacts before she has had time to think; her shoulders harden, her breathing changes, and she begins scanning the room automatically.

Those triggers do not remain just moments of discomfort. In the office where she works as a QA engineer, she has become known for insisting on clear agendas, documented changes, and never being the last person in a conference room. She knows this sounds excessive, but uncertainty itself feels dangerous to her, and sudden movements by other people put her immediately on guard. When a younger male developer once reached across her desk quickly to point at a defect log, she jerked back before she understood why. In those moments she is superalert, watching hands, posture, exits, tone of voice. The physical alarm arrives first, and with it comes the old conviction that she is once again at the mercy of someone stronger, that she will not be able to stop what follows.

The same situations also pull up memory. A cemetery service for an old neighbor recently brought back sharp visual fragments of childhood so vividly that she could see the gray cast of indoor light and the position of a man’s shoes on the floor, yet she felt detached and oddly blank while seeing it. When she is unexpectedly alone with a man, she may later find herself replaying isolated images rather than a continuous account, unable to explain to her husband why she is so shaken. Because these reminders are tied to betrayal and helplessness in her mind, they do more than evoke the past; they revive what she believes the past proved about her. She feels again that she failed to act, that she should have found some way to stop it, and the shame of that conclusion makes the memories harder to put into words, as if language itself stalls where blame begins.

That self-blame has narrowed her world. She increasingly arranges her workday to avoid uncertain encounters, asks to keep her office door open when male coworkers visit, and declines funerals with excuses about fatigue. Her husband has noticed that she studies unfamiliar men in restaurants and flinches at abrupt gestures. Elena understands that most of these people are not dangerous, but what frightens her most is how quickly her mind and body return to the certainty that danger is already here. Each fresh episode seems to confirm the belief that she is still vulnerable and still unable to protect herself, which leaves her feeling both ashamed and watchful.

She sought help after a funeral this spring. Standing near the grave, surrounded by grieving people, she became aware of a man moving in beside her and felt the old jolt surge through her before she could think. Later, trying to explain it, she could only produce disconnected visual details and then went numb. She told her husband she was tired of living as if the past could break through any ordinary moment. What she fears most is that she will spend the rest of her life braced for something she cannot prevent. What she hopes, cautiously, is to understand why these moments still have such power and to stop feeling that the frightened child in those images is all she has ever been.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows triggers leading to threat and memory, but does not clearly state within one paragraph that triggers directly lead Elena's negative appraisals or self-blaming beliefs.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette describes Elena's beliefs about danger and helplessness, but does not clearly convey in one paragraph that these negative appraisals make situations become triggers or reminders.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: Although shame and self-blame are linked to how memories are experienced, the vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that Elena's negative appraisals directly drive or bring up the trauma memory.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette links threat to hypervigilance and old convictions, but does not clearly convey in one paragraph that the sense of threat itself leads to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Over the years, Elena came to believe that bad things happen without warning and that she cannot stop them. Uncertainty has become especially difficult for her.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
When a meeting changed without explanation or a man in a dark suit came into view at a cemetery, the thought arrived almost with the sensation itself: this is what her life is, being caught off guard and unable to protect herself. Each reminder seemed to tell her again that she was still the child who had failed to stop what happened.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Over the years, Elena came to believe that bad things happen without warning and that she cannot stop them. Uncertainty has become especially difficult for her.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Once she was certain that danger announced itself only after it was too late, ordinary ambiguity started to snag her attention in a way it never had before. A postponed conversation, an unexplained change in a room, a man lingering in a doorway could all become charged because her own conclusions had taught her to treat uncertainty as a warning.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The same situations also pull up memory. A cemetery service for an old neighbor recently brought back sharp visual fragments of childhood so vividly that she could see the gray cast of indoor light and the position of a man’s shoes on the floor, yet she felt detached and oddly blank while seeing it.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
What made those images grip so hard was the meaning she still gave them: proof that she had been helpless and had somehow failed. The more she returned to that conclusion, the more easily the old scenes came forward, as if her mind kept retrieving evidence for the case against her.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
In those moments she is superalert, watching hands, posture, exits, tone of voice. The physical alarm arrives first, and with it comes the old conviction that she is once again at the mercy of someone stronger, that she will not be able to stop what follows.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Feeling her body surge like that has gradually become its own kind of proof for Elena that she is permanently vulnerable. The sheer force of the alarm convinces her, in the moment and afterward, that she is not someone who gets to feel safe.
<<<END>>>
